# Dead reckoning (course, speed, time; log line and traverse table) (`dead_reckoning_log_line`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by magnetic_compass, magnetic_declination, map_projection_charts
- Core idea: For each leg, advance from the last position in the estimated direction of travel by speed multiplied by elapsed time. Keep a compass course, time the watches with half-hour sandglasses, and measure speed with a log line: throw a wooden board (the chip) over the stern on a line knotted at regular intervals and count the knots running out while a small sandglass runs (for a 28-second glass about 14.4 m between knots gives speed in nautical miles per hour, 'knots'). Add every leg on the chart or with a table (the Venetian toleta de marteloio, 1436) and correct whenever a latitude or a landfall is known; errors grow by several per cent of the distance run because currents and leeway are invisible.
- Pitfalls:
  - Ignoring current and leeway; the Gulf Stream or Canary Current can move a ship 50–100 km a day without anyone noticing
  - Forgetting the compass variation in every leg
  - Assuming medieval pilots had no way of judging speed; pilots estimated it by eye, with errors that accumulated over a crossing
  - Using knots per hour (a knot already is a speed)
- History: europe: c. 1270–1300 – Mediterranean pilots reckon with compass and chart; 1338 first image of a sandglass (Lorenzetti, Siena); 1436 Andrea Bianco's toleta de marteloio; 1574 William Bourne describes the log and line in print; china: c. 1100 – Song pilots steer by compass and keep rutters of courses and distances; global: Pacific – Polynesian and Micronesian navigators track progress mentally against star and island bearings (etak)
- Read:
  - William Bourne, A Regiment for the Sea (1574)
  - E. G. R. Taylor, The Haven-Finding Art: A History of Navigation from Odysseus to Captain Cook (1956)
